name: Ptosis surgery for asymmetry

lead: Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid. Surgery raises the lower-set lid so the eyes look more alike and more open, and in looksmaxxing discussions it is cited as a way to fix eye asymmetry.

Techniques include shortening the levator muscle, resecting Muller's muscle, or suspending the lid from the forehead muscle (frontalis sling) when the lid muscle is very weak. Surgical series describe it as an established treatment for mild to severe ptosis, with outcomes that vary by cause and technique, and case series of minimally invasive suspension report short recovery.

paras: It is performed by an oculoplastic or eyelid surgeon, usually under local anaesthesia, with the technique matched to how weak the lid muscle is. Swelling and bruising settle over a few weeks and the result is visible once healed.

Reported complications include uneven lids after surgery, dry eye if the eye does not close fully, bleeding, infection, rarely loss of lid movement, and recurrence. Underlying causes such as myasthenia gravis are assessed separately.

angle.text: Eyelid surgery lifts a lower-set upper lid so both eyes open to a similar height and look more alike and more open. It is an established procedure for ptosis, and the change is visible once healed.

lead: Ptosis surgery lifts a drooping upper eyelid so the eye opens fully and matches its partner. When one lid sits lower than the other, the face reads as uneven and the eye can look smaller or sleepy; repairing the lid is how people with noticeable lid asymmetry aim for a more symmetrical, more open and alert eye area. [1][2]

Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid, caused by dysfunction of the levator muscle, its nerve supply, or the sympathetic supply to Muller's muscle, with causes including aging, congenital factors, trauma and conditions such as myasthenia gravis. [1] Surgical options include levator resection or advancement, Muller's muscle resection and frontalis or Whitnall slings. [1][3]

Plastic-surgery reviews describe repair as both a functional and a cosmetic problem, with growing patient demand for an optimal cosmetic result. [4] Brow position is evaluated alongside the lids, because brow shape influences upper lid fold height and crease curvature. [5]

paras: Ptosis is classified as neurogenic, myogenic, aponeurotic, mechanical or neurotoxic; pseudoptosis describes apparent drooping caused by poor lid support or a higher lid on the opposite side.[1] Congenital ptosis is often linked to reduced or absent levator function, while the most common acquired form is aponeurotic, in which the levator tendon stretches or detaches, often with ageing.[1] Neurogenic causes include third-nerve palsy, Horner's syndrome and myasthenia gravis, and neurotoxic causes include botulinum toxin and some snake venoms; high-dose opioids and, mildly, pregabalin have also been linked to drooping lids.[1]

Signs include a lid edge that partly covers the pupil, a reduced gap between the lids, a raised brow with forehead wrinkling as the frontalis muscle compensates, a chin-up head posture, and an absent or poor upper lid crease. Drooping that worsens through the day suggests myasthenic ptosis.[1] Surgeons measure the marginal reflex distance (pupil centre to upper lid edge) and levator function (lid travel from downgaze to upgaze with the brow held still) to choose a procedure.[1]

Eyelid height is one of the first things people notice when comparing the two sides of a face. A drooping lid makes one eye look smaller, tired or sleepy, can leave the brow raised on that side as the forehead muscle compensates, and shows up as asymmetry in photographs.[1][2] People pursuing facial balance therefore discuss ptosis repair alongside eyelid and brow procedures, and plastic-surgery reviews treat the repair as both a functional and a cosmetic problem.[4]

Surgeons evaluate brow position alongside the lids because brow shape influences upper lid fold height and crease curvature, and brow ptosis can mimic or accompany lid ptosis.[5] Wikipedia's article on ptosis gives the aponeurotic type as the commonest acquired form, with mean age at presentation near 68, whereas congenital ptosis presents in childhood.[1]

Levator resection is generally used when levator function is 5 mm or less, and Muller's muscle resection is another option. A frontalis sling is described as preferred in oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy and considered most effective for moderate to severe congenital ptosis, while a Whitnall sling is often chosen when cosmetic appearance is the priority.[1] Children are usually not operated on until about age 4 or 5.[1]
A 2019 series described minimally invasive conjoint fascial sheath suspension for mild to moderate unilateral or bilateral blepharoptosis, intended to shorten recovery and avoid conspicuous scars.[6]

A 2021 review describes posterior Muller muscle-conjunctival resection as a choice for mild to moderate ptosis with good levator function, noting predictable cosmetic outcomes and a lower reoperation rate, while external levator resection is preferred with lesser levator function or ocular surface disease. [3] A randomized trial compared external levator advancement with Muller muscle-conjunctival resection in mild to moderate aponeurotic ptosis with good levator function. [7] A 2018 review notes that innovations over recent years have focused on refining established methods and treating more severe conditions. [8]
Wikipedia also lists non-surgical supports for those who do not have surgery: ptosis crutches attached to glasses and scleral contact lenses.[1]

In 2020 the FDA approved 0.1 percent oxymetazoline ophthalmic solution for acquired blepharoptosis in adults; it is thought to act on alpha-adrenergic receptors in Muller's muscle to lift the lid.[1][9] In the two six-week phase 3 trials, randomised 2:1 against vehicle, the drops produced significant improvements in upper eyelid elevation and in the superior visual field at days 1 and 14.[9] A pooled safety analysis of four randomised, double-masked trials in 568 participants (median age 66, 74.8 percent women) found treatment-emergent adverse events in 31.2 percent of those on oxymetazoline and 30.6 percent on vehicle, with punctate keratitis the most common ocular event at 3.5 percent versus 2.1 percent.[9] The effect is a lift that lasts while the drops are used and is reported for acquired ptosis in adults rather than the congenital form.

Complications include uneven eyelids after surgery, dry eyes if closure is incomplete, bleeding and infection, and rarely loss of lid movement. In one study cited on Wikipedia, half of patients needed further surgery within 8 to 10 years.[1]

Severe untreated ptosis in children can cause amblyopia or astigmatism, which is why early treatment is recommended in young patients.[1] Wikipedia lists dry eye after surgery among complications, and notes that ptosis unrelated to major disease does not shorten life expectancy.[1]

The word ptosis comes from the Greek for "fall." Wikipedia notes historical and modern figures with ptosis, among them Phineas Gage after his 19th-century iron-rod injury and King Edward I of England, whose ptosis it describes as inherited from his father.[1] Oxymetazoline eye drops became the first FDA-approved drug treatment for acquired ptosis in 2020, adding a non-surgical route to a field historically dominated by levator and sling procedures.[1][9]

A randomized clinical trial of 2018 compared external levator advancement with Muller muscle-conjunctival resection for aponeurotic ptosis, with eyelid height (marginal reflex distance) at one month as the primary outcome. [7] A 2022 systematic review of pediatric repair covered 23 studies and 730 patients, mostly case series, and reported reoperation rates averaging about 17 percent for external levator resection and 22 percent for internal approaches, with commonest complications not sight-threatening. [10] A 2018 systematic review of frontalis-orbicularis muscle advancement found 38 articles, many case series with varied techniques. [11] A 2019 series described conjoint fascial sheath suspension for mild to moderate blepharoptosis. [6] No studies found on ptosis surgery framed specifically as looksmaxxing asymmetry correction. Registered phase 3 and pooled analyses of oxymetazoline drops for acquired ptosis reported lid elevation and visual-field gains versus vehicle.[9]
